script.title: Why Robert Maillart Made Concrete Arches Hollow

lines: An engineer walked out across his new concrete bridge to test it.
Robert Maillart rarely tested his bridges before building them.
He often tested them by crossing them himself.
German engineers built elaborate math methods and felt they needed no real load tests.
But that math could not fully analyze unusual shapes.
World War One caught him and his family in Russia.
In 1917, the revolution took his projects.
He came home to Switzerland penniless and deep in debt.
But his best designs were still to come.
Maillart stood back and used common sense.
He joined the road deck and the arch into one thin piece of reinforced concrete.
Concrete took the squeezing. Steel bars took the pulling.
And his hollow box technique could cross large spans.
You see, it's like an empty cardboard box, light, but hard to twist.
His Salginatobel bridge design was picked from among 19 entrants, partly for its low cost.
In 2001, a British trade journal voted it the most beautiful bridge of the century.

claims.claim: Maillart rarely tested his bridges prior to construction; only upon completion would he verify the bridge was adequate, and he often tested his bridges by crossing them himself.

German engineers had developed elaborate mathematical techniques and were confident they did not need practical load tests; those techniques did not encourage unusual shapes because such shapes could not be completely analyzed.
A traditional method prior to the 1900s was to use shapes that could be analyzed easily using mathematics; this overuse of mathematics annoyed Maillart.

Maillart was caught in Russia with his family by World War I; in 1916 his wife died, and in 1917 the revolution caused him to lose his projects; he returned to Switzerland penniless and heavily in debt, but the best of his designs were still to come.
Maillart preferred to stand back and use common sense to predict full-scale performance.
Maillart designed arches in which the deck and the arch ribs were combined into closely integrated structures of very thin reinforced concrete.
In reinforced concrete, the concrete carried compressive forces while steel bars carried the tension forces.
Maillart's hollow-box technique is used to overcome large spans.
A box girder forms an enclosed tube with multiple walls and better resists torsion than an I-beam.
Maillart's Salginatobel design was selected from among 19 entrants in a design competition in part because of the low cost of his proposal.
In 2001 the British trade journal Bridge - Design and Engineering voted Maillart's Salginatobel Bridge the most beautiful bridge of the century.

cast.wife: a 40 year old Swiss woman, slender, a gentle pale heart-shaped face, light auburn hair in a low bun, wearing a long dusty rose wool dress with a cream lace collar, 1910s
cast.german: a 60 year old German engineering professor, heavy build, a bald head with a grey fringe, a full square grey beard, gold pince-nez glasses, wearing a black frock coat with a stiff high white collar, 1910s
cast.worker: a 25 year old Swiss construction worker, lanky, a freckled face, straw blond hair under a flat grey wool cap, wearing a rust red work shirt with rolled sleeves and grey canvas trousers with braces, 1920s
